collision-model-s1.title: Molecular energies at two temperatures
collision-model-s1.text: The graph shows how the kinetic energies of the molecules in a gas are spread out at two temperatures, T₁ and T₂. The same gas sample is used for both. The reaction the gas undergoes has an activation energy of 20 kJ/mol.

collision-model-s2.title: Two collisions with the same energy
collision-model-s2.text: Molecules of NOCl hit chlorine atoms. In the reaction NOCl + Cl → NO + Cl₂, the Cl atom must take the chlorine atom of NOCl. Both collisions below have more than enough energy.
collision-model-s2.html: Key: O, oxygen atom; N, nitrogen atom; Cl, chlorine atom. Arrows show the direction the lone Cl atom is moving.

items.q: Which temperature is higher, and how does the graph show it?
options: T₂: its curve is flatter and spread to higher energies
T₁: its curve has the taller peak
T₁: more of its molecules have low energies
T₂: its curve holds more molecules in total

why.correct: At a higher temperature the average kinetic energy is larger, so the distribution shifts right and spreads out; with the same number of molecules, its peak is lower. That describes T₂.
options: Right: shifted and spread toward higher energy.
A taller, narrower peak at low energy means a lower temperature.
Many molecules at low energy means a lower average kinetic energy, so a lower temperature.
It is the same sample, so both curves represent the same number of molecules (equal areas).

items.q: The reaction is faster at T₂. Which explanation uses the graph correctly?
options: At T₂ more of the molecules have 20 kJ/mol or more
At T₂ the activation energy is lower than 20 kJ/mol
At T₂ each molecule has at least 20 kJ/mol
At T₂ the molecules are smaller and fit together more easily

why.correct: The area under each curve to the right of 20 kJ/mol is the fraction of molecules with enough energy to react. It is much larger for T₂, so a larger fraction of collisions succeeds.
options: Right: more of the curve lies beyond the activation energy.
Heating does not change the activation energy; it changes how many molecules can reach it.
Even at T₂, many molecules have less than 20 kJ/mol; the curve starts near zero.
Temperature does not change the size of molecules.

items.q: Raising the temperature makes molecules collide more often, and makes collisions more energetic. Which effect is larger for most reactions, and why?
options: The energy effect: the fraction above Ea grows fastest
The collision-frequency effect: faster molecules meet each other far more often
The two effects are about equal in size for most reactions
Neither: temperature changes the rate by changing the activation energy

why.correct: A modest rise in temperature raises the collision frequency by a few percent, but it can multiply the fraction of molecules with energy above Ea several times over (compare the tails of the two curves beyond 20 kJ/mol). The energy effect dominates.
options: Right: the high-energy tail grows sharply.
Collision frequency does rise, but only a little compared with the growth of the high-energy tail.
The energy effect is much larger for reactions with a significant activation energy.
The activation energy is a property of the pathway; heating does not change it.

items.q: On the graph, what represents the fraction of molecules that have enough energy to react at T₁?
options: The area under the T₁ curve to the right of 20 kJ/mol
The height of the T₁ peak
The energy at which the T₁ curve peaks
The area under the T₁ curve to the left of 20 kJ/mol

why.correct: The area under a distribution curve between two energies is the fraction of molecules with energies in that range. Molecules beyond 20 kJ/mol can react if they also collide with the right orientation.
options: Right: the tail beyond the activation energy.
The peak height is the fraction at the most common energy, not a count above Ea.
The peak energy is the most probable energy, which is well below Ea here.
Those are the molecules without enough energy to react.

items.q: Which collision can lead to reaction, and why?
options: Collision 1: the Cl atom strikes the Cl end of NOCl
Collision 2: the Cl atom strikes the O end, which is more reactive
Both: each one has more than enough energy
Neither: Cl atoms need a third particle to react

why.correct: To form Cl₂, the incoming Cl must meet the Cl of NOCl. A collision at the O end, however energetic, puts the atoms in the wrong places, so the molecules bounce apart.
options: Right: enough energy and the right orientation.
The O end is far from the Cl atom that must be taken, so this orientation cannot make Cl₂.
Energy is necessary but not enough; orientation matters too.
The step is bimolecular; two particles are enough.

items.q: Only a small fraction of collisions in a gas cause a reaction, even when the gas is hot. Which statements explain this? Select all that apply.
options: Many colliding pairs have less than the activation energy
Many collisions have the wrong orientation
Each molecule collides about once per second
Molecules lose a little mass each time they collide

why.correct: A collision is effective only if it has at least the activation energy and the right orientation. Most collisions miss one or both.
options: Right: not enough energy.
Right: wrong orientation.
Gas molecules collide billions of times per second; the rate limit is not the number of collisions.
Mass is conserved in collisions.

items.q: The gas mixture is heated from 300 K to 320 K with the same container. Predict each change.

variables.name: Number of collisions per second
variables.why: Faster molecules meet more often (a small increase).

variables.name: Fraction of collisions with energy at or above Ea
variables.why: The energy distribution shifts toward higher energy, so more of it lies beyond Ea.

variables.name: Activation energy
variables.why: Ea is a property of the reaction pathway, not of the temperature.

variables.name: Fraction of collisions with a suitable orientation
variables.why: Orientation depends on the shapes of the molecules, not on how fast they move.

why.correct: Heating raises both the collision frequency and the share of energetic collisions; the activation energy and the orientation requirement stay the same.

items.q: Which conditions must a collision meet to cause a reaction?
options: Enough energy and a suitable orientation
Energy of at least Ea, with any orientation
A suitable orientation, with any amount of energy
The two molecules have the same mass

why.correct: The collision model needs both: enough energy to break and rearrange bonds, and the right atoms facing each other.
options: Right: both conditions.
Energy alone is not enough; the wrong orientation bounces apart.
Orientation alone is not enough; a gentle bump does not break bonds.
Mass is not a requirement for an effective collision.

items.q: Food spoils more slowly in a refrigerator. Which explanation uses the collision model correctly?
options: At lower temperature fewer collisions have enough energy to react
Cold temperatures raise the activation energy of the spoiling reactions
Cold molecules stop moving, so they no longer collide
Cold air contains fewer molecules of oxygen per liter

why.correct: Lower temperature shifts the energy distribution to lower energies, so a much smaller fraction of collisions reaches Ea, and the spoiling reactions slow down.
options: Right: fewer energetic collisions.
The activation energy is set by the reaction pathway; temperature does not change it.
Molecules still move at refrigerator temperatures; they just move more slowly.
Cold air is slightly denser, which would speed reactions with oxygen, not slow them.

items.q: Two reactions run at the same temperature. Reaction X has Ea = 40 kJ/mol and reaction Y has Ea = 90 kJ/mol. Other factors are similar. Which statement is correct?
options: X is faster: more collisions reach its smaller Ea
Y is faster: its higher Ea gives each collision more energy
They have the same rate, since the temperature is the same
X is faster, since its molecules collide more often

why.correct: At one temperature the energy distribution is the same, so a larger fraction of molecules is above 40 kJ/mol than above 90 kJ/mol. More effective collisions means a faster reaction and a larger k.
options: Right: lower barrier, more successful collisions.
Ea is a barrier to overcome, not energy given to the molecules.
Same temperature does not mean same rate; the barriers differ.
Ea does not change how often molecules collide.

items.q: A reaction in solution goes faster when the concentration of a reactant is raised, at constant temperature. Which part of the collision model explains this?
options: More particles per liter collide more often each second
Each collision has more energy at higher concentration
The activation energy falls at higher concentration
More particles per liter means each has the right orientation

why.correct: Concentration changes how often particles meet, not how hard they hit. More collisions per second means more effective collisions per second, at the same fraction.
options: Right: collision frequency rises.
Energy per collision depends on temperature, not concentration.
Ea does not depend on concentration.
The fraction with a good orientation is unchanged; only the number of collisions rises.

items.q: For a reaction, 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ of all collisions have enough energy, and of those, 0.15 have a suitable orientation. In 1.0 L, 3.0 × 10³¹ collisions happen each second. How many effective collisions occur per second?

mistakes.why: Value: include the orientation factor too. Only 0.15 of the energetic collisions are oriented correctly.
Value: include the energy factor too. Only 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ of collisions have enough energy.

why.correct: Effective collisions = (total collisions) × (fraction with enough energy) × (fraction correctly oriented) = (3.0 × 10³¹ s⁻¹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁵)(0.15) = 9.0 × 10²⁵ per second.

items.q: A student says, "Heating a reaction mixture lowers the activation energy, which is why it speeds up." Which response is best?
options: Ea is unchanged; more molecules now reach it
Correct: heating lowers Ea and makes collisions more frequent
Ea rises when heated, but collisions become more frequent
Heating speeds a reaction just by making molecules collide more often

why.correct: Activation energy belongs to the reaction pathway. Heating shifts the distribution of molecular energies so that a larger fraction of collisions clears the same barrier.
options: Right: same barrier, more molecules over it.
The barrier is not lowered by heat; that is the misconception.
Ea does not change with temperature in either direction.
Collision frequency rises only slightly; the big effect is the energy distribution.

items.q: A student grinds a solid reactant into a fine powder before adding it to a solution. According to the collision model, what changes?
options: More reactant particles are exposed, so collisions per second rise
Each collision now has more energy, so more of them react
The activation energy is lower for the small grains
The particles in the powder are oriented better

why.correct: Only particles at the surface of a solid can collide with the dissolved reactant. Grinding exposes far more of them, so the number of collisions per second rises; the energy of each collision and Ea are unchanged.
options: Right: more surface, more collisions.
Collision energy depends on temperature, not on particle size.
Ea is a property of the reaction pathway; grinding does not change it.
Grinding changes how many particles are exposed, not how each collision is aimed.

items.q: Two reactions have the same activation energy and are run at the same temperature and concentrations. In reaction 1 two small, round atoms combine; in reaction 2 a small molecule must hit one particular atom on a large molecule. Reaction 1 is much faster. Which explanation fits the collision model?
options: In reaction 2 most energetic collisions hit the wrong part of the large molecule
In reaction 2 the collisions carry too much energy, so the particles bounce apart
Large molecules collide with less kinetic energy at any temperature
Small atoms have a lower activation energy than large molecules

why.correct: With the same barrier and temperature, the same fraction of collisions has enough energy. The difference is orientation: a round atom can react from any side, but only collisions that strike the one reactive atom of a large molecule can work.
options: Right: the orientation requirement is much stricter for reaction 2.
Extra energy does not stop a reaction; a poor orientation does.
At one temperature, all particles share the same average kinetic energy.
The stem says the activation energies are equal.
